_note: Curated from the published record, not produced by our code. Every 'reported' figure
is the authors' own headline number on their own network, demand and simulator.
They are NOT a common benchmark and must never be ranked against each other or
against ours as though they were: the column exists to show what is claimed and
under what assumptions, which is the comparison that actually matters here.
Fields: sensing = what the controller is assumed to know about the emergency
vehicle; conflicts = whether simultaneous requests from conflicting approaches are
handled; guarantees = worst-case properties that hold for any input; hardware =
what has to be installed, and on what, for the method to run at all.

entries.label: Optical preemption (Opticom, deployed)
entries.venue: In field use since the 1970s; Denver Fire Department evaluation, 1977
entries.sensing: Line-of-sight infrared strobe on the vehicle, receiver on the mast
entries.conflicts: First-come-first-served; later requests queue or are ignored
entries.guarantees: None beyond the controller's own clearance intervals
entries.hardware: Emitter on every emergency vehicle, receiver and card in every cabinet
entries.reported_metric: emergency response time along the corridor
entries.network: 3 fire stations, 75 signalised intersections, two 90-day periods
entries.notes: The field baseline the whole area is measured against. Range is the reported minimum and maximum reduction across corridors; the single value is their midpoint and is plotted only for scale. Requires line of sight, so it degrades in curves, heavy rain and dense urban canyons, and reviews of the area name simultaneous conflicting requests as an unresolved operational problem.

entries.label: EMVLight (Su et al.)
entries.sensing: Exact emergency-vehicle position and route, known to the controller
entries.conflicts: Not addressed; the framework is posed around a single emergency vehicle
entries.hardware: V2I link or equivalent position feed from every emergency vehicle
entries.network: 5x5 synthetic grid and a 16x3 Manhattan network, multi-intersection
entries.notes: Also reports 23.5% improvement for non-emergency vehicles. Couples dynamic routing with signal control, which is a strictly larger action space than ours: part of the reported gain is re-routing the vehicle, not re-timing the signal. The closest work in ambition, and the clearest illustration of the assumption we drop.

entries.label: Informed preemption (FLAIRS 2024)
entries.sensing: Predicted emergency-vehicle trajectory from GPS along a known route
entries.guarantees: Fixed safety margins (8 s green warning, 5 s driving allowance)
entries.hardware: GPS and a data link on every emergency vehicle
entries.reported_metric: time to destination vs no preemption
entries.notes: Explicitly motivated by the cost and unreliability of installed preemption hardware, which is the same gap passive acoustics addresses -- but the proposed replacement is another on-vehicle device.

entries.label: RT-FedFlow
entries.notes: Also reports 13.04% reduction in average intersection delay.

entries.label: Acoustic siren detection + DoA (Banchero et al.)
entries.sensing: Microphone array; detection and direction of arrival, no control
entries.hardware: Microphone array on the receiving vehicle

reported_detail.range_output: three classes (near / medium / far) from harmonic energy ratios

entries.notes: The state of the art in acoustic emergency-vehicle sensing, and the reason the sensing half of this problem is considered solved. It is not solved for signal control: the metric is frame-level classification and bearing, the range output is three bins, and no controller consumes it. What a signal controller needs is a calibrated probability that a vehicle is inbound on a named approach and an arrival time in seconds -- neither of which follows from a 95% F1 on frames.

entries.label: Large-scale siren/road-noise detection (SACNN)
entries.notes: Self-attention CNN on a large siren and road-noise corpus. Establishes that the detection problem is tractable at frame level; says nothing about which approach a siren is on, which is the question a four-armed junction actually poses.

entries.label: CoLight and the pressure family (context, not EV)
entries.sensing: Complete lane-level vehicle counts at every intersection
entries.conflicts: n/a -- no emergency vehicles in the benchmark
entries.reported_metric: network average travel time (no emergency vehicles)
entries.network: Jinan and Hangzhou open benchmarks, CityFlow
entries.notes: Included because it is the reference point for RL traffic signal control generally, and because it makes the omission visible: this literature does not model emergency vehicles at all, so a controller can top these benchmarks while being arbitrarily bad at the problem studied here. Numbers are as tabulated in the common benchmark comparisons, not re-run by us.

entries.label: Safe RL under competing transit priority
entries.conflicts: Priority requests are ranked, not scheduled
entries.hardware: Position feed from every priority vehicle
entries.notes: Scalarises priority into the reward, so the trade-off is fixed by a weight chosen before training and has to be retuned per demand level. This is the design the CMDP formulation here replaces.

entries.label: SIREN-ARC (this work)
entries.sensing: Passive roadside microphones only; no equipment on any vehicle
entries.conflicts: Solved exactly: minimum-cost phase ordering over committed requests
entries.guarantees: Minimum green, full changeover, and a proved bound W_max on how long any movement may be denied service, holding for any belief and any adversarial detector output
entries.hardware: One calibrated microphone per approach mast
entries.reported_metric: emergency stopped delay, measured against fixed-time on identical seeded demand
entries.network: single four-arm intersection, 12 seeds x 3600 s
entries.notes: The improvement is computed by scripts/make_tables.py from results/evaluation_balanced.json and inserted at build time, so the number in the table is the number the code produced.
